title: Sociology Basics
summary: Learn to think sociologically: major perspectives, culture and socialisation, social structure and institutions, stratification and inequality measures, deviance and social control, and social change, urbanisation and globalisation.
audience: Social-science students, community workers, teachers and curious readers

body.p: Sociology studies society: how people live together, how groups and institutions shape behaviour, and how societies change. The sociologist C. Wright Mills called the key skill the "sociological imagination": seeing how personal troubles connect to public issues. One graduate without a job is a personal trouble; millions of unemployed graduates point to the structure of the economy and education system.

list: Functionalism (Durkheim): society is like a body whose parts (family, education, religion) work together to keep it stable.
Conflict theory (Marx and others): society is shaped by inequality and struggle between groups over resources and power.
Symbolic interactionism (Mead, Blumer): society is created through everyday interactions and the meanings people give to symbols and actions.
Feminist perspectives: examine how gender shapes power, opportunity and experience.
African and decolonial perspectives: question theories built only from Western experience and centre African knowledge, such as ideas of communal personhood.

body.tip: For any social issue, ask how each perspective would explain it; you will see it from several angles.

body.p: Culture is the shared way of life of a group: beliefs, values, norms, language, symbols, customs and material objects. Norms are expected behaviours, from informal folkways (greeting elders politely) to formal laws.
Socialisation is the lifelong process of learning culture and becoming a member of society. Agents of socialisation include:

list: Family: the first and often most powerful influence.
Peers: friends shape tastes, language and behaviour, especially in adolescence.
School: teaches knowledge plus discipline, competition and national identity.
Religion: values, rituals and community.
Media and social media: images of success, beauty and belonging.
Workplaces: occupational skills and norms.

body.p: Subcultures (such as youth music scenes) share some distinctive norms; countercultures reject mainstream values. Ethnocentrism judges other cultures by one's own standards; cultural relativism tries to understand practices in their own context, while still allowing ethical judgement about human rights.

body.tip: Notice one norm you follow without thinking; asking where it came from is sociology in action.

body.p: Social structure refers to the relatively stable patterns of relationships in society. People occupy statuses (positions such as student, mother, nurse) and play roles (expected behaviours attached to each status). Role conflict happens when demands clash, such as a working mother facing a sick child on an exam day.

list: Primary groups: small, close and lasting, such as family and close friends.
Secondary groups: larger, goal-oriented, such as workplaces and associations.
Formal organisations and bureaucracies, described by Max Weber, run by rules, hierarchy and specialised roles: efficient but sometimes rigid.

body.p: Social institutions are organised systems that meet basic social needs: family, education, religion, economy, government, health care and media. They shape opportunities and are changed by people over time, for example as families become smaller and more urban or as education expands.

body.tip: When analysing an institution, ask what needs it meets, who benefits and who is left out.

body.p: Social stratification is the ranking of groups in a hierarchy of unequal access to wealth, power and prestige. Inequality can be based on class, gender, race and ethnicity, age, disability, location and more, and these often overlap (intersectionality).

list: Poverty rate: if 300 of 1200 surveyed households fall below the poverty line, the poverty rate is 25%.
Income shares: what share of total income the richest 10% receive compared with the poorest 40%.

The Gini coefficient ranges from 0 (everyone has the same) to 1 (one person has everything). Five people with incomes 1, 2, 3, 4 and 10 have a Gini coefficient of 0.4; one person holds half of the total income of 20.
Southern Africa includes some of the most unequal countries in the world by Gini coefficient.

body.p: Social mobility is movement between social positions, within a lifetime or between generations. Education is often a route upwards, but inherited advantages such as wealth, networks and quality schooling make mobility unequal. Sociologists study how structures such as labour markets and historical injustices (for example colonialism and apartheid) shape life chances.

body.tip: Distinguish inequality of outcome (different results) from inequality of opportunity (different chances); policies address them differently.

body.p: Deviance is behaviour that breaks social norms; crime is deviance that breaks laws. What counts as deviant varies across societies and over time.

list: Strain theory (Merton): deviance arises when people cannot reach culturally valued goals, such as wealth, through legitimate means.
Labelling theory: being labelled deviant ("troublemaker") can push people into deviant identities.
Social learning: deviance is learned from others, like any behaviour.
Control theory: strong bonds to family, school and community discourage deviance.
Conflict perspectives: those with power shape which acts are criminalised and how harshly they are punished.

body.p: Informal control includes gossip, praise and disapproval within families and communities; formal control includes police, courts and prisons. Restorative justice, which brings offenders, victims and communities together to repair harm, draws on traditions in many African and other societies.

body.tip: When you hear a claim about crime, ask who defined the behaviour as a crime and whose behaviour is policed most.

body.p: Societies change through technology, economic shifts, social movements, conflict, migration and environmental change.

Africa is urbanising rapidly. If 45% of a country's 60 million people live in towns and cities, that is 27 million urban residents. Urbanisation brings opportunities (jobs, services, new identities) and challenges (informal settlements, unemployment, pressure on housing and water).

list: Globalisation links societies through trade, media, migration and technology, spreading ideas and products while also creating new inequalities.
Digital technology changes how people work, organise and form relationships.
Social movements, from anti-colonial struggles to movements for women's rights, students and the environment, show how ordinary people drive change.
Demographic change, including young populations and migration, shapes future societies.

body.tip: Choose one change in your community over the last ten years and analyse its causes and effects using what you have learned.
